what_it_does: Modern AI chips can save energy by lowering their voltage and clock speed — a technique called dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS) — but this has historically been done in big chunks (e.g., once per program phase) because changing voltage takes time, and individual AI operations finish faster than the voltage can settle. This paper builds a mathematical model that predicts, for each small AI operation in a workload, whether it is limited by computation or by the speed of fetching data from memory. Operations that are waiting on memory transfers rather than doing math can safely run at lower clock speed without slowing down the overall job, so the system drops voltage and frequency for exactly those operations. By pairing this model with a hardware improvement that speeds up the voltage-change mechanism itself, the paper achieves energy savings at the finest possible granularity — one operation at a time.
